source.title: The Scholars' Line
source.summary: How the four madhabs drew the boundary between permissible credit sales and forbidden riba.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: The Quran bans riba. But what exactly is riba? Is a markup on a deferred sale the same as charging interest on a loan? The Hanafi school allowed bay' bi-thaman ajil, selling goods on credit at a higher price, while drawing a sharp line against lending money for a return. The Hanbalis were stricter, suspecting any time-value premium of concealing riba. The Shafi'is focused on the six commodities mentioned in the hadith. And the Malikis developed the concept of sadd al-dhara'i, blocking the means to forbidden ends. This episode walks through the classical debates on where legitimate commerce ends and prohibited interest begins, showing how these 8th-century discussions still define Islamic banking today.

linkedin.post: The Quran bans riba, but defining its exact boundaries sparked centuries of scholarly debate among Islamic jurists. The four major schools of Islamic law each drew different lines: • The Hanafis permitted bay' bi-thaman ajil — selling goods on credit at higher prices — while strictly forbidding lending money for a return • The Hanbalis took a stricter stance, viewing any time-value premium with suspicion as potentially concealing riba • The Shafi'is focused their analysis on six specific commodities mentioned in prophetic traditions • The Malikis developed the concept of sadd al-dhara'i — blocking the means to forbidden ends These 8th-century debates weren't merely academic exercises. They established the theological and legal foundations that continue to shape Islamic banking products and contracts today. The question remains as relevant now as it was then: where exactly does legitimate commerce end and prohibited interest begin? Listen to the full discussion: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-wd-3
